reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Characterised by multiple intensely pruritic, firm, hyperkeratotic nodules arising from a self-perpetuating itch-scratch cycle
Nodules are typically symmetrical on the extensor limbs and trunk, sparing the mid-back where the hand cannot reach ('butterfly sign')
Excoriation, crusting, and post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation commonly accompany the nodules
It is a reaction pattern rather than a single disease, so an underlying cause of chronic pruritus should be sought
Associated conditions include atopic dermatitis, chronic kidney disease, hepatobiliary disease, thyroid dysfunction, HIV, and, less commonly, lymphoma
Neural hyperplasia and upregulation of itch-related mediators contribute to the persistence and severity of the pruritus
Breaking the itch-scratch cycle is central to management, alongside treating any identified systemic driver
reference.pathophysiology: Prurigo nodularis develops when chronic, intense pruritus drives repetitive scratching and rubbing, producing hyperkeratotic, fibrotic nodules. Persistent mechanical trauma and neuroimmune activation lead to dermal fibrosis, epidermal hyperplasia, and proliferation of cutaneous nerve fibres, with increased expression of pruritogenic cytokines and neuropeptides that sensitise itch pathways. This establishes a self-sustaining itch-scratch cycle. The underlying pruritus may be dermatological, systemic (renal, hepatic, haematological, endocrine), neuropathic, or psychogenic, so the nodules represent a common end-point rather than a distinct primary disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple keratoacanthomas or squamous cell carcinomas
Perforating dermatoses (e.g. acquired reactive perforating collagenosis)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and exclude mimics, including bullous pemphigoid on immunofluorescence
Full blood count and renal and liver function tests to seek systemic causes of pruritus
HIV and, where indicated, hepatitis serology
Screening for lymphoproliferative disease in refractory or atypical cases
Assessment of atopic and psychological contributors
redFlags: Systemic symptoms such as weight loss, night sweats, or lymphadenopathy suggesting lymphoma
Unexplained pruritus pointing to occult renal, hepatic, or haematological disease
Rapidly growing or ulcerated nodules raising concern for malignancy
Severe intractable itch with sleep disturbance and marked impairment of quality of life
reference.prognosis: Prurigo nodularis is typically chronic and difficult to treat, with lesions persisting for months to years; outcome improves when an underlying cause is identified and treated and when the itch-scratch cycle can be interrupted.
pitfalls: Treating the nodules symptomatically without investigating an underlying systemic cause of pruritus
Missing an underlying bullous pemphigoid presenting in a prurigo-like form
Underestimating the psychological impact and role of scratching behaviour
Overlooking malignancy in solitary, rapidly changing, or ulcerated lesions
management: Identify and treat the underlying driver of pruritus, whether dermatological, renal, hepatic, thyroid, HIV-related or haematological
Break the itch-scratch cycle with potent or superpotent topical corticosteroids, often under occlusion, and topical calcineurin inhibitors
Intralesional corticosteroid injection for individual resistant nodules
Antipruritic measures including emollients, topical menthol, sedating antihistamines and neuromodulators such as gabapentinoids
Phototherapy with narrowband ultraviolet B for widespread disease
Systemic or biologic therapy for refractory cases, notably dupilumab, or immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or ciclosporin
Psychological support to address scratching behaviour, with dermatology referral for resistant disease
